MY OWN RESULT (step 11, before comparing with steps 1-4). Date basis: today is Thu 22 Oct 2026 (America/Chicago). Not legal advice; this is a technical citation check.

DERIVED FIGURES (from the task givens, no web source needed)
- Total data: 50 tenants x 200 GB = 10,000 GB = 10 TB.
- Peak load: 5,000 queries/min / 60 = 83.3 queries/s, across all 50 tenants combined.
- Per-tenant average peak: 83.3 / 50 = about 1.67 queries/s.
- These are the givens that steps 2-4 cost assumptions must match: 10 TB, 83.3 QPS, HA (Multi-AZ or regional HA).

WHAT I ACTUALLY VERIFIED
Step 2 (AWS RDS/Aurora)
- I fetched the AWS RDS for PostgreSQL pricing page [S115]: https://aws.amazon.com/rds/postgresql/pricing. It resolved. The fetch timestamp was 2026-10-23T04:29:24+00:00, which is 22 Oct 2026 evening in Chicago. The tool returned only the first 6,000 of 28,306 characters.
- The part I read held navigation and general text. A later grep for db.r / db.m instance names and $ prices returned only the T4g/T3 "Unlimited mode" CPU-credit note [S121]. I saw no instance-class price, GB-month price, I/O price or backup price in the visible text.
- So I cannot confirm any specific RDS or Aurora dollar figure. Any such figure in step 2 stays UNVERIFIED by me, not "pass".
- The AWS page is the right official source type. Pricing for eu-central-1 and us-east-1 is usually loaded by script (price list JSON). The static text may not show it. I did not fetch the AWS price-list files, so I cannot say the page supports the figures.

Step 1 (benchmarks)
- I ran web_search on PostgreSQL vs MongoDB benchmarks. Plain code split the queries into several searches. I did not read the result excerpts closely enough to record any title, URL, publication date, sponsor or headline figure with an [S#].
